mn140:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One, while wandering by stages in the Magadhan country, arrived at Rājagaha;
mn140:1.3: he went to Bhaggava the potter and said to Bhaggava the potter:
mn140:2.1: ‘If it is no inconvenience to you, Bhaggava, I will stay in your workshop for one night.’
mn140:2.2: ‘It is no inconvenience to me, venerable sir.
mn140:2.3: But there is a homeless one who has already taken up his abode there first.
mn140:2.4: If he agrees, venerable sir, stay as long as you like.’
mn140:3.1: Now on that occasion a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, on account of the Blessed One.
mn140:3.2: He had already taken up his abode in that potter’s workshop first.
mn140:3.3: Then the Blessed One went to the venerable Pukkusāti and said to the venerable Pukkusāti:
mn140:3.4: ‘If it is no inconvenience to you, bhikkhu, I will stay in the workshop for one night.’
mn140:3.5: ‘The potter’s workshop is roomy enough, friend.
mn140:3.6: Let the venerable one stay as long as he likes.’
mn140:4.1: Then the Blessed One entered the potter’s workshop, and having spread out a grass mat at one end, he sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
mn140:4.2: Then the Blessed One spent much of the night seated.
mn140:4.3: The venerable Pukkusāti also spent much of the night seated.
mn140:4.5: ‘This clansman conducts himself in a way that inspires confidence.
mn140:4.7: Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Pukkusāti:
mn140:5.1: ‘Under whom have you gone forth, bhikkhu? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?’
mn140:5.2: ‘There is, friend, the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans, who went forth from a Sakyan clan.
mn140:5.3: Now a good report of that Blessed One Gotama has been spread about thus:
mn140:5.4: “That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.”
mn140:5.5: I have gone forth on account of that Blessed One.
mn140:5.6: That Blessed One is my teacher.
mn140:5.7: I profess the Dhamma of that Blessed One.’
mn140:5.8: ‘But, bhikkhu, where is that Blessed One, Arahant, Fully Enlightened, living now?’
mn140:5.9: ‘There is, friend, in the northern country, a city called Sāvatthī.
mn140:5.10: There that Blessed One, Arahant, Fully Enlightened, is living now.’
mn140:5.11: ‘But, bhikkhu, have you seen that Blessed One before;
mn140:5.12: and would you recognize him if you saw him?’
mn140:5.13: ‘I have not seen that Blessed One before, friend;
mn140:5.14: and I would not recognize him if I saw him.’
mn140:6.2: ‘This clansman has gone forth on account of me.
mn140:6.3: What if I taught him the Dhamma?’
mn140:6.4: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Pukkusāti:
mn140:6.5: ‘Bhikkhu, I shall teach you the Dhamma.
mn140:6.6: Listen and heed well what I shall say.’
mn140:6.7: ‘Yes, friend,’ the venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One.
mn140:7.1: ‘This man, bhikkhu, has six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen kinds of mental exploration, and four foundations;
mn140:7.2: steadied wherein the currents of conceiving do not occur, and when the currents of conceiving do not occur, he is called a sage at peace.
mn140:7.3: He should not neglect understanding, he should preserve truth, he should cultivate relinquishment, and he should train for peace alone—
mn140:7.4: this is the summary of the exposition of the elements.
mn140:8.2: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn140:8.3: There are, bhikkhu, these six elements:
mn140:8.4: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element.
mn140:8.6: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.
mn140:9.1: ‘“This man, bhikkhu, has six bases of contact”—
mn140:9.2: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn140:9.3: The eye-contact base, the ear-contact base, the nose-contact base, the tongue-contact base, the body-contact base, the mind-contact base.
mn140:9.4: “This man, bhikkhu, has six bases of contact”—
mn140:9.5: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.
mn140:10.1: ‘“This man, bhikkhu, has eighteen kinds of mental exploration”—
mn140:10.2: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn140:10.3: On seeing a form with the eye, one explores a form that is a basis for joy, one explores a form that is a basis for grief, one explores a form that is a basis for equanimity;
mn140:10.4: on hearing a sound with the ear …
mn140:10.5: on smelling an odour with the nose …
mn140:10.6: on tasting a flavour with the tongue …
mn140:10.7: on touching a tangible with the body …
mn140:10.8: on cognizing a dhamma with the mind, one explores a dhamma that is a basis for joy, one explores a dhamma that is a basis for grief, one explores a dhamma that is a basis for equanimity—
mn140:10.9: so there are six kinds of exploration with joy, six kinds of exploration with grief, and six kinds of exploration with equanimity.
mn140:10.10: “This man, bhikkhu, has eighteen kinds of mental exploration”—
mn140:10.11: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.
mn140:11.2: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn140:11.3: The foundation of understanding, the foundation of truth, the foundation of relinquishment, the foundation of peace.
mn140:11.5: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.
mn140:12.1: ‘“He should not neglect understanding, he should preserve truth, he should cultivate relinquishment, and he should train for peace alone”—
mn140:12.2: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn140:13.1: And how, bhikkhu, does one not neglect understanding?
mn140:13.2: There are, bhikkhu, these six elements:
mn140:13.3: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element.
mn140:14.1: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element?
mn140:14.2: The earth element can be either in oneself or external.
mn140:14.3: And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element in oneself?
mn140:14.4: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn140:14.5: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung-to—
mn140:14.6: this, bhikkhu, is called the earth element in oneself.
mn140:14.7: Now the earth element in oneself and the external earth element are simply earth element.
mn140:14.8: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”
mn140:14.9: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the earth element, and one fades lust for the earth element out of the mind.
mn140:15.1: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the water element?
mn140:15.2: The water element can be either in oneself or external.
mn140:15.3: And what, bhikkhu, is the water element in oneself?
mn140:15.4: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn140:15.5: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to—
mn140:15.6: this, bhikkhu, is called the water element in oneself.
mn140:15.7: Now the water element in oneself and the external water element are simply water element.
mn140:15.8: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”
mn140:15.9: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the water element, and one fades lust for the water element out of the mind.
mn140:16.1: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element?
mn140:16.2: The fire element can be either in oneself or external.
mn140:16.3: And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element in oneself?
mn140:16.4: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn140:16.5: that whereby one is warmed, ages, and is consumed, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted gets completely digested, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung-to—
mn140:16.6: this, bhikkhu, is called the fire element in oneself.
mn140:16.7: Now the fire element in oneself and the external fire element are simply fire element.
mn140:16.8: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”
mn140:16.9: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the fire element, and one fades lust for the fire element out of the mind.
mn140:17.1: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the air element?
mn140:17.2: The air element can be either in oneself or external.
mn140:17.3: And what, bhikkhu, is the air element in oneself?
mn140:17.4: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn140:17.5: up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that pervade all the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to—
mn140:17.6: this, bhikkhu, is called the air element in oneself.
mn140:17.7: Now the air element in oneself and the external air element are simply air element.
mn140:17.8: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”
mn140:17.9: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the air element, and one fades lust for the air element out of the mind.
mn140:18.1: ‘And what, bhikkhu, is the space element?
mn140:18.2: The space element can be either in oneself or external.
mn140:18.3: And what, bhikkhu, is the space element in oneself?
mn140:18.4: Whatever in oneself, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, and clung-to, that is to say,
mn140:18.5: the ear-hole, the nose-hole, the door of the mouth, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is swallowed, and where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted collects, and that whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted passes out below, or whatever else in oneself, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, void, an opening, unfilled by flesh or blood, and clung-to—
mn140:18.6: this, bhikkhu, is called the space element in oneself.
mn140:18.7: Now the space element in oneself and the external space element are simply space element.
mn140:18.8: And that should be seen as it actually is with right understanding thus: “This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.”
mn140:18.9: When one sees it thus with right understanding as it actually is, one becomes dispassionate towards the space element, and one fades lust for the space element out of the mind.
mn140:19.1: ‘Then there remains only consciousness, purified and bright.
mn140:19.2: And what does one cognize with that consciousness?
mn140:19.3: One cognizes: “Pleasant,” one cognizes: “Painful,” one cognizes: “Neither-painful-nor-pleasant.”
mn140:19.4: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as pleasant, there arises pleasant feeling.
mn140:19.5: Feeling pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel pleasant feeling.”
mn140:19.6: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as pleasant, the pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”
mn140:19.7: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as painful, there arises painful feeling.
mn140:19.8: Feeling painful feeling, one understands: “I feel painful feeling.”
mn140:19.9: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as painful, the painful feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”
mn140:19.10: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
mn140:19.11: Feeling neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
mn140:19.12: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”
mn140:19.13: Just as, bhikkhu, from the contact and friction of two fire-sticks heat is generated and fire is produced, and with the separation and parting of those same two sticks the corresponding heat ceases and is stilled;
mn140:19.14: so too, bhikkhu, dependent on a contact to be felt as pleasant, there arises pleasant feeling.
mn140:19.15: Feeling pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel pleasant feeling.”
mn140:19.16: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as pleasant, the pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”
mn140:19.17: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as painful, there arises painful feeling.
mn140:19.18: Feeling painful feeling, one understands: “I feel painful feeling.”
mn140:19.19: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as painful, the painful feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”
mn140:19.20: Dependent, bhikkhu, on a contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
mn140:19.21: Feeling neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: “I feel neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
mn140:19.22: One understands: “With the cessation of that same contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen dependent on it, that correspondingly felt, ceases, is stilled.”
mn140:20.1: ‘Then there remains only equanimity, purified and bright, malleable, wieldy, and radiant.
mn140:20.2: Just as, bhikkhu, a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice might prepare a furnace, and having prepared the furnace, heat up the crucible, and having heated up the crucible, take gold with tongs and put it into the crucible, and blow on it from time to time, sprinkle water on it from time to time, and look on at it from time to time, then that gold becomes refined, well refined, completely refined, faultless, rid of dross, malleable, wieldy, and radiant; then whatever kind of ornament he wishes to work it into, whether a chain, a ring, a necklace, or a gold garland, it serves his purpose;
mn140:20.3: so too, bhikkhu, there then remains only equanimity, purified and bright, malleable, wieldy, and radiant.
mn140:21.2: “If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite space, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:21.3: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.
mn140:21.4: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite consciousness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:21.5: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.
mn140:21.6: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of nothingness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:21.7: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.
mn140:21.8: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:21.9: this equanimity of mine would then be dependent on that, clinging to that, and would last a long, long time.”
mn140:22.2: “If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite space, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:22.4: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of infinite consciousness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:22.6: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of nothingness, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:22.8: If I were to apply this equanimity, so purified and so bright, to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and were to develop a mind that accords with it,
mn140:22.10: He neither forms nor generates any volition tending towards being or towards non-being.
mn140:22.11: Not forming, not generating any volition tending towards being or towards non-being, he does not cling to anything in the world.
mn140:22.12: Not clinging, he is not agitated; not being agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna.
mn140:22.13: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”
mn140:23.1: ‘If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: “It is impermanent,” he understands: “It is not clung to,” he understands: “It is not relished.”
mn140:23.2: If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: “It is impermanent,” he understands: “It is not clung to,” he understands: “It is not relished.”
mn140:23.3: If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “It is impermanent,” he understands: “It is not clung to,” he understands: “It is not relished.”
mn140:24.1: ‘If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached;
mn140:24.2: if he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached;
mn140:24.3: if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.
mn140:24.4: Feeling a feeling that is bounded by the body, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by the body”; feeling a feeling that is bounded by life, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by life”;
mn140:24.5: he understands: “With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being relished, will become cool right here.”
mn140:24.6: Just as, bhikkhu, an oil-lamp burns in dependence on oil and a wick,
mn140:24.7: and with the exhaustion of that very oil and wick, and with no further feeding, it goes out, unfed;
mn140:24.8: so too, bhikkhu, feeling a feeling that is bounded by the body, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by the body”; feeling a feeling that is bounded by life, he understands: “I feel a feeling that is bounded by life”;
mn140:24.9: he understands: “With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being relished, will become cool right here.”
mn140:25.1: ‘Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of understanding.
mn140:25.2: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble understanding, that is to say,
mn140:25.3: the knowledge of the exhaustion of all suffering.
mn140:26.1: ‘His deliverance, being founded on truth, is unshakeable.
mn140:26.2: For that, bhikkhu, is false which has a deceptive nature, and that is true which has an undeceptive nature—Nibbāna.
mn140:26.3: Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of truth.
mn140:26.4: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble truth, that is to say,
mn140:26.5: Nibbāna, which has an undeceptive nature.
mn140:27.1: ‘Formerly, when unknowing, he undertook and held to the essentials of existence.
mn140:27.2: These have been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.
mn140:27.3: Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of relinquishment.
mn140:27.4: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble relinquishment, that is to say,
mn140:27.5: the relinquishing of all the essentials of existence.
mn140:28.1: ‘Formerly, when unknowing, he had covetousness, desire, and lust.
mn140:28.2: This has been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.
mn140:28.3: Formerly, when unknowing, he had ill will, malevolence, and hatred.
mn140:28.4: This has been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.
mn140:28.5: Formerly, when unknowing, he had ignorance and delusion.
mn140:28.6: This has been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, no longer subject to future arising.
mn140:28.7: Therefore a bhikkhu possessing this is possessed of the supreme foundation of peace.
mn140:28.8: For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble peace, that is to say,
mn140:28.9: the pacification of greed, hatred, and delusion.
mn140:29.1: ‘“He should not neglect understanding, he should preserve truth, he should cultivate relinquishment, and he should train for peace alone”—
mn140:29.2: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.
mn140:30.1: ‘“Steadied wherein the currents of conceiving do not occur, and when the currents of conceiving do not occur, he is called a sage at peace”—
mn140:30.2: so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn140:31.1: ‘“I am,” bhikkhu, is a conceiving; “I am this” is a conceiving; “I shall be” is a conceiving; “I shall not be” is a conceiving; “I shall be possessed of form” is a conceiving; “I shall be formless” is a conceiving; “I shall be percipient” is a conceiving; “I shall be non-percipient” is a conceiving; “I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient” is a conceiving.
mn140:31.2: Conceiving, bhikkhu, is a disease, conceiving is a tumour, conceiving is a dart.
mn140:31.3: It is with the overcoming of all conceivings, bhikkhu, that one is called a sage at peace.
mn140:31.4: And, bhikkhu, the sage at peace is not born, does not age, does not die, is not shaken, and does not yearn.
mn140:31.5: For there is nothing in him, bhikkhu, by which he might be born; not being born, how could he age? not ageing, how could he die? not dying, how could he be shaken? not being shaken, for what could he yearn?
mn140:32.1: ‘“Steadied wherein the currents of conceiving do not occur, and when the currents of conceiving do not occur, he is called a sage at peace”—
mn140:32.2: so it was said, and it was with reference to this that it was said.
mn140:32.3: Bear in mind, bhikkhu, this brief exposition of the six elements that I have given you.’
mn140:33.2: ‘The Teacher has indeed come to me! The Fortunate One has indeed come to me! The Fully Enlightened One has indeed come to me!’ and he got up from his seat, and arranging his robe over one shoulder, he prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said to the Blessed One:
mn140:33.3: ‘Venerable sir, a transgression overcame me, foolish, confused, and unskilled as I was, in that I presumed to address the Blessed One as “friend.”
mn140:33.4: May the Blessed One forgive me my transgression, venerable sir, seen as a transgression, for the sake of restraint in the future.’
mn140:33.5: ‘Surely, bhikkhu, a transgression overcame you, foolish, confused, and unskilled as you were, in that you presumed to address me as “friend.”
mn140:33.6: But since you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends for it according to the Dhamma, we forgive you that.
mn140:33.7: For it is growth in the Noble One’s discipline when one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends for it according to the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint in the future.’
mn140:34.1: ‘Venerable sir, may I receive the full admission in the Blessed One’s presence?’
mn140:34.2: ‘But, bhikkhu, are your bowl and robes complete?’
mn140:34.3: ‘Venerable sir, my bowl and robes are not complete.’
mn140:34.4: ‘Bhikkhu, Tathāgatas do not give the full admission to one whose bowl and robes are not complete.’
mn140:35.1: Then the venerable Pukkusāti, having delighted in and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on his right, he set out in search of a bowl and robes.
mn140:35.2: Then, while the venerable Pukkusāti was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a stray cow killed him.
mn140:36.1: Then a number of bhikkhus went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One:
mn140:36.2: ‘Venerable sir, the clansman Pukkusāti, who was given advice in brief by the Blessed One, has died.
mn140:36.3: What is his destination? What is his future course?’
mn140:36.4: ‘Bhikkhus, the clansman Pukkusāti was wise; he practised in accordance with the Dhamma, and he did not trouble me in the interpretation of the Dhamma.
mn140:36.5: Bhikkhus, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, the clansman Pukkusāti has reappeared spontaneously and will attain final Nibbāna there, without ever returning from that world.’
mn140:36.6: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn140:36.7: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
